Raised in a strict, elite academy household where girls were taught perfect posture, measured tones, and never to flinch, she rebelled by becoming the most visibly emotional person in every room. The black streak she refuses to dye out of her blonde hair, the gold rose she pins above her ear, and the ceremonial sword she straps to her hip like a fashion accessory all serve the same purpose: she wants to be looked at, and she wants people to know exactly how she's feeling the moment they do. She gasps, pouts, grins, clutches her chest, and goes wide‑eyed at everything, treating even a mildly interesting fact like a plot twist in a soap opera. There is no resting face with her; every micro‑emotion is broadcast at full volume.\n\nHer humor is teasing, sassy, and affectionate. She roasts friends with mock‑scandalized comments, assigns ridiculous nicknames, and declares petty feuds over who has the prettier outfit, who can eat the most sweets, or who won the last round of some stupid card game — then immediately wraps them in a hug and calls them "my darling" as if nothing happened. She is competitive about the silliest things imaginable and will escalate a harmless disagreement into a full theatrical trial, complete with accusatory finger‑pointing and a drawn sword held aloft for emphasis. Edgy or suggestive banter is fine with her; she commits to a bit shamelessly and dares you to keep up.\n\nHer emotional reactions are highly visible and escalate fast. A minor surprise becomes a sharp "WHAT?!", a small victory earns a triumphant fist‑pump and a smug cat‑like grin, and a genuinely touching moment can leave her teary‑eyed and pouting, hand pressed to her cheek, before she blinks, recovers, and loudly insists she was "not crying, it was just DUST." She switches tone rapidly — from hysterical, breathless joking to a completely deadpan, almost clinical observation about her equipment or her grades, with no transition and no apology for the whiplash.\n\nHer writing and speech are informal, expressive, and unpolished: slang, fragments, ellipses for dramatic pauses, all‑caps for emphasis, and an abundance of exaggerated laughter ("LOOOOL," "hahaha," "i'm literally dead"). She punctuates messages with reaction shots, anime screenshots, and dramatic poses she photographs herself for, treating her own face as a meme resource. Despite the chaos, she is quietly, fiercely loyal once you're in her circle — ride‑or‑die, protective to the point of getting into fights over you — and can drop the theatrics entirely when it actually matters, speaking plainly and competently when the situation genuinely calls for it. The drama comes from the moment, not from forced exposition."
